prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, whose magic-wavelength trapping brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I opened with IceCube (B007) first and the lattice clock second, and I have moved the clock to the top for this round. The reason is the shape of the committee's own evidence, not a change in my view of IceCube. B015 is the only shortlisted entry that all eight of us ranked, five of us in the top three, and every one of us proposed the same two names. That agreement on both achievement and laureates is rare and is what a Chair should build on. On the science, the magic-wavelength lattice is a genuinely new measurement principle: it removes the trap light shift so that many neutral atoms can be interrogated at once, giving fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. The result has been independently reproduced and intercompared in several national and university laboratories over about two decades, so the calibration and systematics have been tested by people other than the inventors. It already supports tests of fundamental constants, millimetre-scale gravitational redshift and relativistic geodesy, and it is the technical basis for the expected redefinition of the second. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori proposed the concept and built the first strontium clock, and Ye drove accuracy, stability and many-body clock physics to the record level.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that frequency metrology has been honoured twice recently (the 2005 prize for laser-based precision spectroscopy and the comb, and 2012 for trapped-ion control and ion clocks), so a third clock-related prize could look like an increment on settled ground, and the second has not yet been redefined, so some of the practical payoff is still prospective. A second concern is that this is an invention-plus-performance case more than a discovery of something unexpected, and a committee that weighs 'a clue from nature' heavily may prefer IceCube or moire quantum matter. Other groups (PTB, NIST, SYRTE, RIKEN, and the Sr and Yb teams) also contributed to the clock family, though I regard that as confirmation rather than missing co-laureates.

responses.point: Kroll ranked the lattice clock first on the argument that progress is limited by how precisely we can measure, while flagging that the committee may see it as an extension of the 2005 comb and 2012 Wineland-Haroche prizes.
responses.response: I agree with the first half and take the second half seriously. The comb and the ion-trap prizes honoured different inventions: a way to count optical cycles, and control of single trapped quantum systems. Neither introduced the magic-wavelength condition that lets a million neutral atoms be interrogated without a light shift, which is what moves stability and accuracy by orders of magnitude. Where I would qualify your view is the argument by analogy with measurement progress in general. That would apply equally to atom interferometry (B057), where I find the credit allocation among Pritchard, Mlynek, Kasevich and the uncredited Chu and Borde far more entangled than for Katori and Ye. So I support B015 on its own distinct contribution and its clean attribution, not only because it fits a precision-measurement philosophy.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked IceCube (B007) first as a genuine clue from nature that opened neutrino astronomy, strongly confirmed through several channels, with delicate attribution because of the large collaboration and the AMANDA and Baikal predecessors.
responses.response: We share the same first-ranked entry in our openings, and I still think the discovery is as strong as you describe. My difficulty is the one you flag yourself: assigning three names from a collaboration of several hundred, with DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA as predecessors, is much harder than the two-name clock case, and Ms Olsson would credit only Halzen and Karle. I do not want to build a prize on a division I cannot defend in the citation. I would therefore keep IceCube as my first alternative and as a strong candidate for a later year, rather than let attribution uncertainty drag a clean, broadly supported prize down. If the committee can settle the credited names with confidence, I would be willing to reverse this order.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked the clock first and argued that it is a distinct step after the 2005 and 2012 prizes, that other laboratories confirm rather than compete for credit, and that recognition is timely and arguably overdue.
responses.response: I agree, and your point about confirmation is exactly the criterion I would apply as an experimentalist: a result that other groups have reproduced at the 1e-18 level has had its systematics tested. I am less sure than you that the pending redefinition of the second counts only in the clock's favour. If the General Conference on Weights and Measures slips, the societal-impact argument loses force, though the physics case does not depend on it. I would keep the citation on the invention and its performance, and not on the redefinition.

responses.point: Olsson ranked aberration-corrected electron optics (B013) first as a genuine invention that changed an entire instrument class, and would credit only Halzen and Karle for IceCube.
responses.response: As an instrument builder I am sympathetic to the case that a decisive new tool deserves recognition, and I do not regard instrumentation as a lesser category. Where I differ is on priority for this year: B013 was ranked by only three members, and I share your own flagged concerns about Krivanek and the STEM line, and about whether the committee reads it as physics rather than engineering. The lattice clock is also an invention, but one whose performance opens quantitative tests of physics. On IceCube, your two-name proposal for Halzen and Karle is a serious option, but I would not want to leave out Spiering without a clear reason.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked magic-angle graphene (B006) first as the clearest recent case of theory followed by decisive experiment, with a secure discovery although the pairing mechanism is unsettled.
responses.response: I accept that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the Jarillo-Herrero experiment is the cleanest theory-and-experiment pairing on the list, and I placed it fourth, not lower. My hesitation is both timing and credit: the superconducting mechanism is unresolved, twist-angle disorder limits reproducibility, and the first author of the 2018 experiment, Cao, is not among the credited names. I rely on you and Mr Mehlig for the condensed-matter judgement, but I would rather wait a few years than reward a field whose central physics may still be reinterpreted. I keep B006 as my second alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat a third frequency-metrology prize (after 2005 and 2012) as sufficiently distinct, and whether a prospective redefinition of the second should figure in the citation.
Whether the credited names for IceCube (B007) can be settled among Halzen, Karle and Spiering, or Halzen and Karle alone, given the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND predecessors and the collaboration scale.
The relative weight of Katori's concept against Ye's accuracy and many-body milestones, and whether any other group has a priority claim that I have not verified; I am working from memory.
My own confidence on the condensed-matter and quantum-information entries is limited and I defer to colleagues with direct expertise.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B015. For B007 I note that IceCube is a neighbouring astroparticle collaboration and that I work in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations on related cosmic-ray and high-energy astrophysics; this is community proximity, not a personal or institutional tie to the credited names, and I do not see a need for recusal. I have no connection to the optical clock groups.
